title: They lived
hook: Jews lived full lives in Europe's cities and towns

segments.voice: Yesterday, a doorway and a word, Shoah, and your line: go gently. Keep it close. Today begins where yesterday promised, with life.

A black-and-white photo. A boy on a bicycle on a cobbled street, grinning, his cap pushed back. Behind him a shop sign in Hebrew letters, a woman leaning out of a window, two men arguing on a corner with their hands. Nobody in the picture is posing for history. They're just having a Tuesday. It's easy to meet the Jews of prewar Europe only through how their world ended. This session meets them first as they were: alive, busy, and not waiting for anything.
screen: `A BOY ON A BICYCLE.` → `JUST HAVING A TUESDAY.` → `MEET THEM AS THEY WERE.`

segments.voice: Jewish Europe was not one place. It was big cities: Warsaw, Vilna, Budapest, Berlin, Amsterdam, Salonika, Paris. And it was small market towns across Eastern Europe, the kind Yiddish calls a shtetl, a little town, where Jews and their neighbors traded on market day. It was not one kind of Jew either. There were Hasidim gathered around their rebbes, singing at long tables. There were yeshiva students arguing over the Talmud late into the night. There were Jewish socialists organizing unions, and Zionists, from the last few lessons, learning Hebrew and dreaming of the land. There were Jews who kept little of the tradition and thought of themselves as Germans or French. There were Yiddish newspapers and theaters, poets and comedians, soccer clubs and summer camps, doctors, tailors, scholars, grocers, and children doing homework at kitchen tables. They fell in love. They fought about politics. They worried about rent. They celebrated weddings and argued with their grandparents. Photographers walked those streets, and some of their pictures survive, faces looking back across the years. The Torah has a line, spoken by Moses at the edge of the land, setting life and death before the people: "therefore choose life." This lesson is a small choice like that. Before the next sessions tell what was done to these communities, they deserve to be met alive. Not as victims first. As neighbors, with Tuesday plans. They lived.
screen: `CITIES AND SMALL TOWNS.` · `MANY KINDS OF JEWS.` · `LOVE, POLITICS, RENT, WEDDINGS.` · then, large: `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Hold one old photo of a community, a family picture if you have one, or simply the boy on the bicycle. Choose one face and wonder about one ordinary thing: what they ate that day, what made them laugh, who they were going home to. Give them a whole life in your mind, not just an ending.
They lived. The Jews of prewar Europe, in cities and small towns, of every kind, met first as people living full lives. Today's word.
Your line: just having a Tuesday. Bakeries, arguments, weddings, rent: life, in full. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Museums, archives and Jewish communities collect photographs, letters and memorial books from prewar Jewish towns and cities, so that remembrance includes how people lived, not only how they died.
